The Chamber of Deputies definitively approved the bill on antisemitism on Tuesday evening, 17 November, with 147 votes in favour, 93 against and 5 abstentions, writes Il Post. The Senate had already approved it in March; according to Euronews, the vote then was 105 in favour, 24 against and 21 abstentions. All opposition amendments were rejected. The Five Star Movement, the Green and Left Alliance and the Democratic Party, which had abstained in the Senate, voted against; the centre-right, +Europa, Italia Viva and Azione voted in favour, reports Il Post.

The text, promoted by the League's group leader in the Senate Massimiliano Romeo, adopts as a reference the definition of antisemitism by the IHRA, the intergovernmental alliance for Holocaust remembrance. According to Il Post, it does not introduce new crimes or prohibitions and clarifies the conduct that Italy has already been countering since 2020. Among the IHRA's examples are the denial of the Jewish people's right to self-determination and holding them collectively responsible for the actions of Israel.

For critics, the definition may confuse antisemitism with criticism of Israel and limit the possibility of criticising its policies, writes Il Post, which reports the assessment of Amnesty International: «a dark day for freedom of expression». Those who oppose it called for the 2021 «Jerusalem Declaration», which does not consider criticism of Israel based on evidence to be antisemitic. Livia Ottolenghi, president of the Union of Italian Jewish Communities, expressed great satisfaction, according to Il Post. The law does not need to return to the floor.

The European Commission has proposed a new loan of up to €45 billion for Ukraine, intended for 2027. It is in addition to the €90 billion already approved for 2026 and 2027. The proposal is preliminary and must be approved by the European Parliament and the Council.

The proposal decides who finances Ukraine's defence and budget in 2027 and how long the common debt would remain the responsibility of the member states. The Ukrainian government says that with rising costs, another €70 billion is needed for 2027. The EU would cover two-thirds of that deficit, while allies such as the United Kingdom, Norway, Canada, Japan, and Australia would have to provide the remaining €25 billion.

Of the €45 billion, about €25 billion is for the purchase of weapons and about €20 billion for civilian expenses such as schools and hospitals. The loan would be financed with common debt: the Commission would issue bonds on behalf of all member states. Commission officials estimate interest of about €6 billion per year on the total loans, which member states would cover with subsidies so that they do not burden Ukraine.

Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Bulgaria have indicated that they will not participate, and Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico is opposed. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has threatened to veto the next EU budget if the 27 do not support the loan. The Commission is offering the four countries the option to join the €20 billion civilian portion and remain outside the €25 billion military portion.

Ukraine would only repay if Russia accepted war reparations in a future peace agreement; until then, the EU would renew the loan. The EU reserves the right to use frozen Russian assets, about €210 billion, for repayment.

The International Court of Justice, the UN's main court, ruled today in The Hague that Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya. The decision passed by 9 votes to 6 and concerns the Rohingya group in the north of Rakhine State, in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

For the first time, the Court has recognised a State as responsible for genocide. The ruling is final and cannot be appealed. Jurist Toby Cadman said that enforcement will depend on subsequent steps, such as intervention by the UN Security Council or sanctions.

The Court found that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of civilians, committed widespread sexual violence and also targeted those fleeing towards Bangladesh. The text cites evidence of approximately 10,000 Rohingya killed. The judges wrote that the only reasonable deduction from the atrocities is the intention to destroy a substantial part of the group. They added that Myanmar has failed to fulfil its obligation to prevent genocide.

The case was brought by The Gambia in 2019. Myanmar denies the accusation: it says that the 2017 offensive was a response to attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army on police posts. The offensive pushed at least 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh. According to the UN, over 1.3 million Rohingya are displaced in the region, 1.2 million of whom are in Cox's Bazar.

There are no comments from the Myanmar government nor measures imposed by the Court.

On 15 November the Yashar and Likud teams met without making progress, according to the Times of Israel, which adds that Netanyahu is reportedly open to excluding Ben Gvir and that parallel talks between Eisenkot's bloc and United Torah Judaism are reportedly making headway, which the party's leader denies.

The United Kingdom had announced a similar plan in 2022, later abandoned by Keir Starmer's Labour government due to legal obstacles, Open recalls; Prime Minister Andy Burnham, according to the same source, says he is following the European initiative with interest. Marine Le Pen, candidate of the Rassemblement national (RN) for the 2027 presidential election, presented her pension plan on Tuesday, 17 November. She promises to abolish on 1 January 2028 the reform that raises the legal age to 64, which was suspended in 2025, write France 24 and franceinfo.

The retirement age would return to 62 and drop to 60 for those who start working early. According to France 24, those who enter the workforce before the age of 20 would retire at 60 with 160 quarters; from 23 years onwards, at 62 with 168. Franceinfo adds that a quarter would be valid with at least part-time work, without a salary threshold, and that the criteria for arduous work would be eliminated. The two outlets provide different figures on the penalty for missing quarters: 2.5% for France 24, 5% for franceinfo, both with a 50% cap.

A new feature is a mandatory capitalisation pillar. According to the RN dossier cited by France 24, it would provide about €340 more per month for a full career at the minimum wage. Franceinfo estimates €12 billion per year, managed by the Caisse des dépôts, with a return of 4-6%, and a cost for the reform of €10.1 billion. Le Monde writes that the funding penalises precarious workers and the housing fund.

Le Pen does not rule out a referendum if she does not have an absolute majority in the Assembly. According to France 24, the text does not guarantee the system's balance; Jean-Philippe Tanguy, of the RN, deems long-term forecasts «unreasonable».

The Rome public prosecutor's office has opened a file on Futuro Nazionale, the party founded by Roberto Vannacci. The file is registered as a «model 45»: there are no suspects and no crime has yet been formally recorded, meaning it is an investigation without a hypothesis of a crime.

The case concerns a party active in political debate and the application of a law that has had few precedents. Anti-terrorism prosecutor Simona Marazza, who is handling the file, must decide whether there are grounds to open criminal proceedings.

The file stems from a complaint filed on 28 August by the Military Union, led by Luca Marco Comellini. The hypothesis indicated in the complaint is the violation of the Scelba Law, which prohibits the reorganisation of the fascist party. The complaint also cites propaganda and incitement to hatred, incitement to commit a crime and disobedience to the laws, and asks to verify whether the movement is subversive.

The complaint is based on public statements, political proposals and content on social media, including images generated with artificial intelligence, on the proposal for «remigration» and on security measures such as red zones without an expiry date.

Vannacci's lawyer, Giorgio Carta, says that the accusations are «completely unfounded». The military prosecutor's office in Rome, led by Marco De Paolis, had launched preliminary investigations in September into serving military personnel who allegedly hold roles in the party's local committees, and had stated that it was not investigating Vannacci for the reorganisation of the fascist party.
